analysis.one_liner: Raises federal tobacco taxes sharply and spends 3% of new revenue helping tobacco farmers switch to other crops.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 15, 1995, never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Bill Bradley proposed raising federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, and roll-your-own tobacco — for example, taking the cigarette tax from $12 to $62 per thousand, which works out to roughly $1.24 more per pack on top of the existing tax. Ninety-seven percent of the new revenue would flow to the general Treasury, while 3% would go to a new Tobacco Conversion Trust Fund paying tobacco farmers to switch to other crops and giving grants to tobacco-dependent communities to diversify their economies. The bill never moved after being referred to the Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, most directly the estimated hundreds of thousands of people who studies show would quit or never start smoking when prices rise sharply, plus their families who avoid secondhand smoke; taxpayers benefit from new federal revenue; and tobacco farmers and their communities would get paid help converting to other livelihoods rather than being left to absorb the shock alone.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal cigarette tax from $12 to $62 per thousand (about $1.24 more per pack), a large enough price increase that economists and public health researchers expect a substantial drop in smoking, which is the leading preventable cause of death in the United States.

Extends and raises taxes across all tobacco products — cigars, snuff, chewing and pipe tobacco, cigarette papers and tubes — and imposes a new tax on roll-your-own tobacco, closing a loophole where rolling tobacco was taxed far less than finished cigarettes.

Creates a Tobacco Conversion Trust Fund funded by 3% of the new revenue to pay tobacco farmers to quit growing tobacco (including government purchase of their tobacco allotments) and to fund economic diversification grants and loans for tobacco-dependent communities.
Imposes the tax on warehouse floor stocks as of January 1, 1996, and on goods entering from foreign trade zones, so retailers and importers could not avoid the increase by stockpiling.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers — who are disproportionately lower-income — would pay the higher taxes at the register; tobacco product manufacturers and wholesale distributors would bear the one-time floor stocks tax and reduced sales; and tobacco farmers would lose sales, though the bill would compensate them through the conversion fund.

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: lower-income smokers spend a larger share of their income on cigarettes, so the biggest direct cost of the bill would fall on people with the least money, even if many of them quit as intended.

The tax is collected on smokers and manufacturers rather than on any penalty for the industry itself, so a manufacturer able to pass through costs or shift sales abroad could cushion its losses while individual smokers bear the burden.

A sudden multi-fold increase could hit adult smokers who do not quit with a large price shock, and tobacco-dependent rural communities would see demand fall faster than the 3% conversion fund could replace it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health upside of a large, sustained price increase on tobacco is well established — price increases reduce smoking, especially among teenagers — and the bill was thoughtfully designed in one respect: it included dedicated money so farmers and tobacco towns would not absorb the entire cost of a public health policy aimed at their livelihood. The regressive incidence is a real drawback, but public health advocates generally accept it because the money saved from quitting dwarfs the added tax for those who quit, and non-smokers pay nothing. On balance a serious, well-targeted bill whose main cost falls on the industry selling the leading cause of preventable death.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 15, 1995, and the committee never took it up; with zero cosponsors and no further action, it died when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Bradley introduced the bill on May 15, 1995; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, distributors, and growers came out ahead: a large tax increase on their product never advanced, and cigarette prices stayed near their historically low federal tax levels. Smokers who continued to smoke were spared the higher price, at the cost of continued smoking-related illness and death.

for.name: Sen. Bill Bradley
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor: introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (104th Congress)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over excise taxes
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 15, 1995 and never reported it out; no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal tobacco tax increases throughout the 1990s and backed lawmakers who blocked them.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Democrat, sponsored the bill and no one from either party cosponsored it, so there is no vote record showing how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: The cigarette tax would have risen more than fivefold, from $12 to $62 per thousand, directly raising the price of their product; tobacco demand is price-sensitive, so this cuts sales. The industry's interest in blocking such taxes runs directly against the public health benefit they would produce.

Higher taxes would reduce demand for their leaf, but the bill would simultaneously pay farmers to exit (including buying out tobacco allotments) and fund diversification grants and loans for their communities — compensation most later tobacco legislation lacked.

industries.industry: Cigar, snuff, chewing and pipe tobacco makers
industries.note: All non-cigarette tobacco taxes rise sharply in the bill (snuff from 36 cents to $16.53 per pound, for example), raising prices across their product lines.
They would owe a one-time tax on warehouse floor stocks on January 1, 1996, designed to prevent stockpiling before the new rates took effect, and would face higher inventory costs afterward.
